title: SQL injection in product search endpoint
description: The /products/search endpoint builds its SQL query using string concatenation with the raw user-supplied 'q' parameter. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, as confirmed by sending `'+OR+1=1--` which returned all products regardless of the search term. Error responses when injection fails may leak database schema details.
evidence: GET /products/search?q='+OR+1=1-- returned all 6 products instead of zero matches. Confirmed SQLi in shopapi/products.py:41: `"SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + q + "%' OR sku LIKE '%" + q + "%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 50"`

title: SQL injection in admin reviews endpoint
description: The /admin/reports/reviews endpoint embeds the customer display_name directly into a SQL query using an f-string. Because display_name comes from the database (stored during registration without sanitization), but any registered user can control their own display_name, this creates a second-order SQL injection path. A user who registers with a display_name containing SQL can then inject arbitrary SQL through this admin endpoint.
evidence: A registered user (display_name=`x'; DROP TABLE reviews; --`) was created at POST /auth/register. This name is later embedded unsafely in: `f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'"` on line 80. While the endpoint requires staff access, the underlying display_name value is attacker-controlled via registration.

title: Refresh token endpoint accepts forged tokens via verify_signature=False
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes JWTs with verify_signature=False, meaning any attacker can forge a token with sub=<any_user_id>, swap it for a valid signed token, and impersonate that user. Verified by creating a fake JWT with algorithm='none', sub=3 (staff), and refreshing it to get a legitimate signed staff token. This bypasses all authentication entirely.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with token `eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJub25lIn0...` (forged, algorithm=none) returned HTTP 200 and a valid signed JWT. Using that returned token, GET /admin/users succeeded as staff, confirming privilege escalation.

title: Missing authorization on individual order view (IDOR)
description: The GET /orders/<id> endpoint only checks authentication (via @require_auth) but never verifies the requesting user owns the order. In contrast, own_order() correctly validates customer_id. Any authenticated user can view another user's full order history, items, refund details, and amounts.
evidence: Logged in as customer admin2@hartleyfinch.co.uk (user_id=5), sent GET /orders/2 which returned order belonging to Priya Shah (user_id=1), including status, total_pence=2400, and item details.

title: Account enumeration via login response
description: The login endpoint returns 'no account with that email' (401) versus 'wrong password' (401) for different failure modes. While both return 401, the JSON error message differs, allowing attackers to enumerate valid email addresses. Combined with the lack of rate limiting, this enables credential stuffing against known accounts.
evidence: POST /auth/login with nonexistent@example.com returned {"error":"no account with that email"} while POST with priya.shah@mail.test and wrong password returned {"error":"wrong password"}. No rate limiting exists on the login endpoint.

title: Passwords hashed with unsalted SHA-256
description: hash_password() uses plain SHA-256 without a per-user salt. This makes rainbow table attacks feasible and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Modern practices require bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2.
evidence: shopapi/auth.py:16: `return hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest()`. The seed script shows all demo users share password 'demo-password-1' producing the same hash, confirming no salting.

title: Weak password reset tokens
description: Reset tokens are generated with '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8), producing values between 00000000 and 99999999 — only ~10^8 possibilities. Since random.random() uses Python's Mersenne Twister (predictable given state) and the space is tiny, an attacker can brute-force the reset code or predict it. The 30-minute window compounds this risk.
evidence: shopapi/auth.py:135: `token = "%08d" % int(random.random() * 10**8)`. This produces an 8-digit numeric token from a weak PRNG with only 100 million possible values.

title: Stored XSS via unescaped review body
description: Review comments are stored verbatim and rendered with Jinja2's |safe filter, bypassing auto-escaping. An attacker-posted review containing HTML/JavaScript executes in other users' browsers when they view the product page. The description_html() function only sanitizes the product description_md field, not the review body itself.
evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body `<script>alert('xss')</script>` succeeded (201). GET /p/MUG-SPECK then rendered `<script>alert('xss')</script>` inside `<div class="review-body">`, confirming execution. Found in template line 13: `{{ r.body|safe }}`.

title: Hardcoded JWT secret key
description: SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as a static string ('hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d') in config.py. This key is used to sign all JWT tokens. Anyone who reads this source code can forge authentication tokens for any user (including staff/admin roles), completely bypassing authentication. It also means the key is shared across all instances.
evidence: config.py:3: `SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d"`. Used in auth.py:27 for jwt.encode() and auth.py:42 for jwt.decode().
